newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries trading higher approaching closing.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries trading higher approaching closing.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were trading higher late Wednesday after recovering from earlier losses on hints of impending inflation.

The Commerce Department reported that it estimated first quarter gross domestic product grew by 5.6 percent, sending bond prices lower. However, inventories grew more than expected and the figure is known to have sharp revisions -- helping to limit bond price deterioration.
The Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond was trading at 95-29/32 late Wednesday, up 13/32 to yield 6.95 percent.

"The Fed doesn't seem to be getting the job done ... they're having a hard time even with the blizzard of activity we've seen" meeting add needs, Pearl said. "We had a popup coupon pass this week no one expected and they may do more."

Pearl said the market was set up for an uptrend and that could occur if payrolls came in below expectations or if there was a downtick in hours worked -- a good possibility considering weather problems during April.
Treasury has reported huge cash balances -- $87.6 billion on Tuesday -- a surge that has exacerbated the Fed's add need and led to optimism on a budget compromise.

Price improvement following the initial selloff after GDP's release was strong as players looked to another possible coupon pass and talk in Washington made it seem likely a balanced budget agreement was imminent. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin also said the federal budget deficit would be substantially lower than expected, making a compromise more politically practible.
"We're looking at sideways trading until payrolls. The technicals are very strong," said Tom Pearl, head repo trader at Chase Securities Inc.
The Federal Reserve continued to have a tremendous add need as strong tax receipts were draining money supply, Pearl said.

Michael Englund, economist at MMS International said the sales component of GDP came in expected, so the market should not have sold off as much as it did initially. The Chicago purchasing managers survey came out strong, but the prices paid component moderated from 57.4 to to 53.3 -- a factor boosting the market.
A rise to 56.1 from in April from 53.4 in the employment component of the index was largely ignored, Englund said.
In addition, budget talks between the White House and Congress were described as being "good and productive" by a Clinton administration spokesman, providing the market with more of a bid.

Englund said weak ECI data had thrown a monkey wrench into many analysts' expectations about labor market conditions, making the nonfarm payrolls report all the more important. Bond prices had not yet fully priced in the good news from ECI, he said.

Englund expected the buildup seen in inventories would translate to GDP growth slowing to 2.0 percent in the second quarter and 1.5 percent in the third. That would give the Fed some leeway to stop tightening monetary policy, but he still expected to see the Fed to do so again at its May meeting.
Further profit-taking was likely to be seen on Thursday ahead of the payrolls report, he said.

Late Wednesday the three-month bill rate was one basis point lower at 5.10 percent. Six-month bill rates were up two basis points at 5.31 percent and year bill rates were down one basis point at 5.57 percent.
Five-year notes were up 08/32 at 100-07/32, yielding 6.57 percent. Ten-year notes were up 09/32 at 96-21/32 to yield 6.72 percent.
